description:
I am a curious person with a strong interest in technology, science, programming, and space exploration. I enjoy learning new things, exploring ideas, and turning challenges into creative solutions. 

Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I hope to put my knowledge into practice, challenge myself, learn from new experiences, and develop solutions that bring technology and science together.
summary:
What we developed: First Footprint is a free web app that ranks every land area on Earth by how closely it resembles the Moon and Mars, explains the score, and shows when real equipment can be tested there.

How it addresses the challenge: We combine seven NASA Earth-observation products (MODIS and MERRA-2) and NASA POWER with Moon and Mars references from NASA missions (LRO Diviner, Curiosity REMS, NASA Fact Sheets). About 30 measured variables give each of 21,306 land cells a 0–1 similarity score for four targets, including the lunar south pole chosen for Artemis. For every site, the app states what matches, how much, and what Earth cannot reproduce, such as gravity. Users then pick a real drone, robot or lander and get the exact days and hours it can operate, from a 16-day forecast or NASA POWER history since 2001.

Why it matters: Without manual tuning, it ranks Atacama, NASA's own Mars test site, first, and reveals less-studied analogs in Asia and Africa. That means safer, cheaper mission rehearsals, open to every country.
details:
Before any robot, drone or astronaut operates on the Moon or Mars, it is tested on Earth, in places called analogs. Today, those places are mostly chosen by habit: the same few famous sites (Atacama, Antarctica, Iceland, Hawaii) are reused, rarely compared with real measurements, and no tool tells teams when the weather will allow a test. First Footprint answers three questions in one free browser app:

1. FIND: Where on Earth is most similar to a given Moon or Mars environment?

2. EXPLAIN: How similar is it, variable by variable, and where does the analogy break?

3. SCHEDULE: When can a specific, real piece of equipment actually operate there?

HOW WE USE NASA DATA

NASA data is the backbone of every number in the app.

- Earth side (what each place is like): we downloaded and processed seven NASA products through NASA Earthdata (earthaccess):

• MODIS Terra MOD08_M3: cloud fraction, aerosol optical depth (550 nm), water vapor

• MODIS MOD13C2: vegetation index (NDVI), mean and maximum

• MODIS MOD11C3: day/night land surface temperature, daily thermal range, extremes

• MODIS MCD12C1: land cover (barren soil, snow/ice, land fraction)

• MERRA-2 FLX, SLV and AER (NASA GMAO): mean and peak wind, annual precipitation, air temperature, relative humidity, surface pressure, dust and aerosols

• Also combined with open non-NASA layers: NOAA ETOPO 2022 (elevation, roughness, slope), GLiM (rock types: basalt, sediments, evaporites), GHSL (population) and WDPA (protected areas).

All layers are harmonized into one global 1° grid (21,306 land cells, ~30 variables per cell).

- Moon and Mars side (the targets): reference values come from NASA missions and references: LRO Diviner (lunar surface temperatures), Curiosity/MSL REMS (Martian surface weather), Mars Global Surveyor TES (Martian surface properties), and the NASA Mars and Moon Fact Sheets (gravity, pressure, temperature).

- Time side (when to test): NASA POWER provides hourly temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation and solar radiation from 2001 to ~3 days ago, letting users replay any past period hour by hour. We use the ratio of actual to clear-sky radiation as a cloud proxy.

- The 3D globe uses NASA Blue Marble imagery.

NASA data does more than set the scene: it is what turns "this desert looks like Mars" into a measured, auditable comparison, which is exactly what the challenge asks for.

HOW THE SCORE WORKS (TRANSPARENT BY DESIGN)

Each target profile (Mars dusty plains like Gale/Jezero, Mars periglacial ground like Phoenix, the lunar south pole targeted by Artemis, lunar mare plains like Apollo 11/15) defines an ideal and a worst value for each variable. Each variable gets a 0–1 score and the profile score is a weighted average. Cells missing more than 40% of the total weight receive no score, so high scores are never built on thin data. In the app, every variable is labeled strong, partial or failing, with its value, target and scientific source. Fixed limits that no Earth site can reproduce (reduced gravity, vacuum or thin atmosphere, radiation) are shown with NASA sources in every analysis. A separate operational score (slope, clouds, wind, rain, aerosols) shows how easy a site is to work in. A population filter (GHSL) keeps only remote areas.

VALIDATION

With no manual tuning, the Mars plains profile ranks Atacama, Chile (0.79) as #1 worldwide. It is the desert NASA already uses to test Mars rovers, which confirms the method. It also surfaces the Qaidam Basin (0.78) and the eastern Tarim Basin and Kumtag Desert (0.76–0.77) in China: sites with nearly the same score that have received far less attention. Agencies' well-known analogs are drawn on the globe for comparison.

SCHEDULING REAL EQUIPMENT

Users pick a preset based on public specifications (DJI Matrice 350 RTK drone, Boston Dynamics Spot robot, SpaceX Falcon 9 launch criteria, Astrobotic Xodiac lander) or enter their own limits (wind, gusts, rain, temperature, humidity, clouds, visibility, dust, slope, sun elevation, required continuous hours). The app tests every hour against those limits and returns operating windows, plus why each failed hour failed:

- Forecast mode: next 16 days (Open-Meteo, with dust from Copernicus CAMS), with windows up to 7 days flagged as reliable.

- History mode: any period from 2001 onward using NASA POWER, with day-by-hour charts and monthly percentages.

- Batch mode: up to 40 random tests across sites and equipment.

Every candidate on the map is colored by feasibility, and all results can be downloaded as CSV.

WHO BENEFITS

- Space agencies and mission planners: choose analog sites with evidence, compare many sites at once, and see each site's limits up front.

- Robot, drone, rover and instrument builders, including startups: know where and when to test before paying for a field campaign, cutting wasted trips and risk.

- Universities and researchers in every country: find a credible, data-backed analog close to home, for free.

- Teachers, students and the public: explore Moon and Mars analogs on an interactive globe, in any browser.

- Beyond space: the same "operating window" logic works for mapping drones, robots in mining, and logistics in extreme environments on Earth.

SOCIAL IMPACT

- Opening space exploration to more countries: today the best-known analogs sit mostly in a few wealthy nations. By ranking the whole planet, First Footprint shows strong candidates in Central Asia, Africa and South America, giving universities and agencies in the Global South a data-backed way to propose their own test campaigns.

- Cheaper, safer missions: testing in the right place, on the right day, reduces failed field trips and catches equipment problems before launch, supporting Artemis and future Mars missions.

- Free and reproducible: all data is open and public, the code is open, and anyone can rerun and check every result.

- Accessible by design: full keyboard navigation, screen-reader support (status, results and dialogs are announced), colorblind-safe Okabe-Ito colors paired with symbols (✓ ! ✕), and a reduced-motion mode.

- Education: a hands-on way to learn how satellites measure our planet and how scientists prepare to explore others.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

To our knowledge, it is the first tool to combine a planet-wide, data-driven analog search with a simulation of real equipment against hourly forecast and historical weather. It turns the question "where should we test?" into "where, how similar, and when?"

HONEST LIMITATIONS

- Earth cannot reproduce Moon/Mars gravity, pressure or radiation; the app states this in every analysis.

- The 1° grid (~110 km) is a screening step; the next step is 30 m terrain data and a site visit.

- The grid climatology uses four months of 2023 (configurable to more months or years).

- Forecasts beyond 7 days are indicative; NASA POWER history lacks gusts, visibility and dust, so those criteria apply only to forecasts.

- Some equipment limits are estimated where manufacturers do not publish them; the app marks every estimated value.

NEXT STEPS

30 m terrain at selected sites, military and other restricted areas, mineralogy from NASA ASTER/EMIT, more months and years in the grid, and new targets such as Europa or Titan by editing a profile file.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Python 3.12, earthaccess (NASA Earthdata), pyhdf, xarray, netCDF4, rasterio, numpy, pandas, pyarrow (Parquet), FastAPI, uvicorn, pydantic, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, globe.gl (three.js). Automated QA with 16 checks against real APIs, plus an offline synthetic test.

SI DISCLOSURE

Claude (Anthropic) was used to help write and debug the code, draft texts, the slide deck and the video script, design the logo (marked "SI-generated" where it appears) and assemble the video edit. ElevenLabs generated the narration voice. All data processing uses real, open datasets; no data was generated by SI.
